qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

Latvia is seeking an additional allocation of approximately EUR 7 billion in the next EU budget. This is intended to cover higher defence spending and the economic consequences of severing ties with Russia. The cost of the policy of cutting ties with Russia is thus beginning to be shifted onto the common European budget. 1.
Does the Commission regard Latvia’s request as an admission that the policy towards Russia is already costing Member States so much that they are unable to bear the costs themselves?
Does the Commission actually intend to give Latvia those EUR 7 billion?
Does the Commission consider it sustainable for every further tightening of policy towards Russia to result in a new request for money from Brussels?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.10.2026) The Commission proposed an ambitious EU budget for an ambitious Europe – designed to deliver on EU priorities and give Europe the capacity to act. Following Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the Commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework1 would support specific needs and challenges of Member States bordering Russia or Belarus, such as Latvia, in the areas of security, border management and economic development. For this reason, under the Commission’s proposal, they benefit from a bonus in the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) allocation key (border management and visa strand of home affairs)2. The NRPPs would also include reforms and investments supporting defense industry, internal security, cybersecurity, border and migration management. The Commission has also proposed a number of actions: 1) via the European Defence Industry Programme3, the European Defence Projects of Common Interest as projects of regional interest, including the Eastern Flank Watch to boost security along the EU’s eastern border. 2) Under the future Connecting Europe Facility4, EUR 17.65 billion for military mobility (10-fold increase), to support dual-use transport infrastructure projects. 3) via the European Competitiveness Fund5 for access to key relevant capabilities and protection of critical military mobility infrastructure, ensuring coordination with sectors like space and civil security, and simplified access to funding. The overall size of the 2028-2034 long-term budget will continue to be discussed in the following months and the requests from Member States regarding funding priorities will continue to be addressed to find common ground.
